extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of poetics; poets, literary critics, and teachers of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles for composing and judging epic and tragic poetry (unity of action, metre, diction, treatment of the irrational, length, episode use, and audience considerations) from a classical poetics perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action (single whole action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot ought, as in a tragedy, to be constructed on dramatic principles: it should have for its subject a single action, whole and complete, with a beginning, a middle, and an end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poem should 'resemble a living organism in all its unity' and produce the pleasure proper to such unity. Avoid making the whole of a vast war or event the subject; detach a single portion instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit scope so beginning and end are in single view
rubrics_metrics.description: The beginning and the end must be capable of being brought within a single view; keep within moderate limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Length should answer to the group of tragedies presented at a single sitting; do not attempt a theme so vast that it cannot be grasped as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of episodes to diversify (but restraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic may detach a single portion and admit as episodes many events from the general story, thus diversifying the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include episodes (e.g., Catalogue of the ships) to relieve sameness and add variety, but avoid over-complication by excessive variety that impedes unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of epic: simple, complex, ethical, pathetic
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic poetry must have as many kinds as Tragedy: it must be simple, or complex, or 'ethical,' or 'pathetic.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate structural/affective mode (simple vs. complex, ethical vs. pathetic) to suit the subject and intended effects (e.g., Odyssey = complex & ethical; Iliad = simple & pathetic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parts required (reversal, recognition, scenes of suffering)
rubrics_metrics.description: The parts (with exception of song and spectacle) are the same as in tragedy: it requires reversals of the situation, recognitions, and scenes of suffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the poem contains the structural incidents that produce tragic/pathetic effects where appropriate (recognition sequences running through a narrative are a feature of complexity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought and diction must be artistic
rubrics_metrics.description: The thoughts and the diction must be artistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction and intellectual content should be crafted artistically; Homer is given as the model in both thought and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic's narrative capacity to enlarge scale appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: Epic has a special capacity for enlarging its dimensions: narrative form allows many events simultaneously transacted to be presented and, if relevant, to add mass and dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the narrative form to present simultaneous or multiple episodes that are relevant to the subject to create grandeur; avoid unrelated multiplicity that weakens unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sameness; vary incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Sameness of incident soon produces satiety and makes tragedies fail on the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary incidents and introduce episodes to prevent monotony; the epic's ability to divert the hearer relieves the story with varying episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate metre: heroic for epic
rubrics_metrics.description: As for the metre, the heroic measure has proved its fitness by the test of experience; narrative poems in other metres would be incongruous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer heroic verse for large-scale epic because it is stately, massive, and admits rare words and metaphors. Avoid mixing different metres (example of Chaeremon criticized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre suitability for other effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Iambic and trochaic tetrameter are stirring measures: the latter akin to dancing, the former expressive of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metre in relation to the kind of imitation: dancing or action-oriented passages may suit other metres, but mixing metres in a great-scale poem is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize authorial intrusion
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak as little as possible in his own person; it is not this that makes him an imitator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bring characters in quickly after few prefatory words; characters should appear with characteristic qualities and not be obscured by frequent authorial commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: distinct ethical character (ethos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be 'each with a character of his own'—none of them wanting in characteristic qualities, but each having a distinct ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present figures with clear, compact traits; avoid vague or unformed characterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of the wonderful and the irrational
rubrics_metrics.description: The element of the wonderful is required in Tragedy; the irrational, on which the wonderful depends, has wider scope in Epic because the person acting is not seen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The wonderful is pleasing and may be used more freely in epic narration (where absurdities may pass unnoticed) but must be handled to preserve poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prefer probable impossibilities to improbable possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When introducing implausible elements, aim for what is plausibly impossible (evokes belief) rather than something unlikely but technically possible; the impossible may be justified if it attains the poetic end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude irrationality from the action
rubrics_metrics.description: Irrational elements should, if possible, be excluded; or at all events, lie outside the action of the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If irrationality is essential it should be placed outside dramatic enactment (example: Oedipus' ignorance of Laius' death), not narrated as part of stage action that would seem absurd.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrationality may be acceptable if made plausible
rubrics_metrics.description: Once the irrational has been introduced and an air of likelihood imparted to it, we must accept it in spite of the absurdity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An adept poet (e.g., Homer) can veil absurdities by poetic charm; lesser poets would make them intolerable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction management: elaborate in pauses, plain in action
rubrics_metrics.description: The diction should be elaborated in the pauses of the action, where there is no expression of character or thought; conversely, character and thought are merely obscured by diction that is over brilliant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve ornate language for moments without character/thought expression; maintain clarity during scenes of character and cognitive content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of imitation and vehicle of expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet must imitate one of three objects—things as they were or are, things as they are said or thought to be, or things as they ought to be. The vehicle of expression is language—current terms or rare words or metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether representation aims at fact, reported belief, or ideal; adjust linguistic choices (register, rare words, metaphor) accordingly; poetic correctness differs from other arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish essential vs accidental poetic faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Within the art of poetry itself there are two kinds of faults—those which touch its essence, and those which are accidental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If incorrect imitation arises from lack of capacity it is an essential error; technical inaccuracies (e.g., in medicine) are accidental. Address objections by considering whether fault touches the essence of the poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify impossibilities only if they serve the art's end
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet describes the impossible he is guilty of an error; but the error may be justified if the end of the art be thereby attained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An impossible element (e.g., Hector's pursuit) may be permitted when it renders some part of the poem more striking; if the same end could be achieved without violating poetic rules, the error is not justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual evaluation of actions and sayings
rubrics_metrics.description: In examining whether what has been said or done is poetically right, we must consider by whom it is said or done, to whom, when, by what means, or for what end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speech/action relative to speaker, addressee, timing, means, and purpose (e.g., whether it secures a greater good or averts a greater evil).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve textual/critical difficulties via linguistic/contextual tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulties may be resolved by regard to accent, breathing, punctuation, ambiguity of meaning, metaphor, usage of language, and dialectal senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret rare words or odd usages by considering metaphor, local usage (e.g., Cretan εὐειδές), accentuation, punctuation, and multiple possible senses; many disputed lines can be clarified this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of criticisms and response strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Critical objections come from five sources: things are censured either as impossible, or irrational, or morally hurtful, or contradictory, or contrary to artistic correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When answering critics, classify objections into these five kinds and seek solutions under the set of interpretive/poetic 'heads' (the text notes twelve possible heads of solution).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mode choice should consider audience refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: If the more refined art is higher, then the more refined mode appeals to the better sort of audience; epic is addressed to a cultivated audience who do not need gesture, tragedy to an inferior public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose epic or tragic mode with respect to intended audience: epic suits a cultivated hearer and can rely on narrative; tragedy involves performance and may aim at a broader or less-refined public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restraint in mime/movement and avoidance of vulgarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all movement is blameworthy, but 'vulgar' or excessive gestures and imitations (e.g., bad flute-players twisting) are signs of unrefined art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that physical representation, mime, and stage movement are appropriate and not merely pandering to dull audiences; avoid imitative extravagance that undermines poetic dignity.
